# One-Pager Workflow-Driven Anonymization for Agent Builder

**Author:** Jon Wålstedt · **Date:** 2026-04-28 · **Status:** Draft companion to the full RFC

---

## The problem

Kibana’s AI agents transmit user data to external LLM providers (e.g., OpenAI, Vertex), which can contain sensitive PII. The legacy anonymization plugin was "heavy," requiring complex profile objects, a persistent replacements index, and a standalone salts service. 

## The solution

We are replacing this now deprecated system with a **workflow-driven architecture** integrated directly into **Agent Builder lifecycle hooks**. This approach performs PII masking in-memory at the inference boundary, ensuring security compliance while eliminating persistent storage overhead. 

### Reusable Building Blocks

Two small, reusable building blocks in a new `kbn-anonymization` package:

1. **An `ai.pii` workflow step** \- runs Named-Entity Recognition (NER) plus regex on natural-language text and returns a token map (e.g. `john@acme.com` → `EMAIL_a3f2c1d8…`).

2. **An `AnonymizingChatModel` decorator** \- wraps any langchain chat model. Outgoing messages are tokenized; the LLM's responses are detokenized before they reach the user or storage.

Agent Builder is the first consumer; other GenAI surfaces (e.g. Security Solution's `elastic_assistant`) can adopt the same primitives the same way.

## How It Works

1. **Detection:** When a user sends a message, the beforeAgent hook runs a user-configured anonymization workflow.

2. **Mapping:** The ai.pii step produces a token map stored in-memory on the per-round RunContext.

3. **Inference:** Every LLM call is wrapped by the decorator; outgoing messages are tokenized so the **LLM sees tokens only**.

4. **Response:** The streaming response is detokenized; the **user and storage see real values**.

5. **Cleanup:** When the round ends, the RunContext is garbage-collected and the map is gone.

## Key design choices

* **Storage holds real values.** Anonymization is an LLM-edge concern, not a storage concern. Conversation history is stored verbatim, so there's nothing to "decode back" when sessions resume.

* **No persistent token storage.** Tokens are deterministic via `HMAC-SHA256(value, conversation_salt)` \- the same input produces the same token on every turn. The only durable artifact is one extra `salt` field per conversation document.

* **Trusted detection backend.** NER runs on an Elasticsearch ML node (Elastic's CoNLL-03 DistilBERT model by default), not on the same external LLM we're hiding data from. A runtime guard rejects any backend that resolves to an external chat-completion endpoint.

* **Fail-closed by default.** If anonymization fails (ML node down, regex timeout, malformed config), the round aborts with a clear error. We never silently ship unredacted PII to the LLM.

* **Configuration is the workflow.** No Stack Management UI, no profile saved-objects, no new plugin lifecycle hooks \- a single YAML file is the entire surface.

* **One decorator covers all LLM call sites.** Agent Builder makes inference calls from at least five places. Wrapping the chat model once per round covers them all uniformly.

## What's explicitly out of scope

* Field-level masking and ES|QL data lineage.  
* A dedicated UI for managing anonymization rules.  
* Storing message history in anonymized form.  
* A new public lifecycle hook (no `afterAgent`, no `beforeInference`).  
* Path-based structured-JSON scrubbing \- `ai.pii` works on natural-language text only.

## What we're removing

* `x-pack/platform/plugins/shared/anonymization` (deprecated plugin)  
* `x-pack/platform/packages/shared/ai-infra/anonymization-common`   
* `x-pack/platform/packages/shared/ai-infra/anonymization-ui`   
* The encrypted `.kibana-anonymization-replacements` index, the salts service, per-space key rotation, and the `xpack.anonymization.active` feature flag

## Why this is the right shape

A user-authored workflow expresses *what* PII to detect. A platform decorator expresses *how* tokens flow through the LLM round-trip. Neither piece needs to know about the other beyond a small, typed context object. The result is a security feature with one configuration file, no new persistence, no new lifecycle hooks, and a clean separation between user policy and platform infrastructure.
